photographs.alt: Top title reads: “C is for CROTAL BELLS” in large, outlined letters. Additional text at the bottom of the page reads: “C is for CROTAL BELLS!” Crotal bells (often called sleigh bells, rumble bells, or jingle bells) have been used for safety purposes for hundreds of years. (Heads up! Horse and carriage—or sleigh—coming through!) Since “Jingle Bells” was written in the 19th century, popular culture has associated them with holiday cheer and winter wonder. These examples are from the archeology collection at Saratoga National Historical Park.” Bottom right corner text reads: “3.” Each of these two, small, round, metal bells has a small loop on top to attach them to a horse’s harness. Made of thin metal, each bell is has two halves, top and bottom, that were attached after a small metal ball, the ringer, was placed inside. Each bell also has a small hole in the side of its top and a small, narrow notch cut in the side of its bottom to help make its ringing sound louder and easier to hear.
photographs.caption: C is for Crotal Bells

photographs.alt: Top title reads: “A is for ASTBURY” in large, outlined letters. Addition text on the bottom reads: “A is for ASTBURY! This cup is from the archeology collection at Salem Maritime National Historic Site. It was used to drink tea about 250 years ago! This kind of delicate, reddish pottery with a shiny glaze is called “Astbury-type,” and it was popular in the 1700s. Bottom right corner text reads: “1.” In the middle of the page is rendering of a large, broken bowl. It is missing a significant portion of the back and bottom. The bowl body has a pattern of four horizontal lines grouped together at the top, a quarter down, three quarters down, and at the bottom. There are two groups of four vertical lines, one at each end. The lip of the bowl is quite large. There are three significant vertical cracks at different parts of the bowl.
photographs.caption: A is for ASTBURY

photographs.alt: Top: “I is for INKWELL” in large outlined letters. Bottom left reads: “I is for...INKWELL! This small inkwell is from the archeology collection at the Abiel Smith School, which was a school for Black children in Boston from 1835 to 1855. The conditions in the school were not as good as conditions in white schools, and many people fought against this injustice. In 1855, the school closed when the state of Massachusetts outlawed separate schools for white and Black children. The outside of this inkwell is made of a soft metal called pewter and the inside is made of glass. It would have fit right into a students desk! Today, the Abiel Smith School is part of the Museum of African American History, a partner of Boston African American National Historic site.” Bottom right corner: “9”. In the center is an outline inkwell and pen. The inkwell shaped like a bucket with a flat lip at the top. Half of a broken lid to the inkwell rests across the top. There is a ink pen drawn at a downward angle in front of inkwell.
photographs.caption: I is for INKWELL

photographs.alt: A letter written on a piece of aged, yellow paper. Header text reads: "S.G. 7506--1895. Department of Justice, Washington, D.C. May 9, 1896. W.J.H." Letter text reads: "James F. Read, Esq., U.S. Attorney, Fort Smith, Ark. Sir: There is pending on the docket of the Supreme Court the case of Crawford Goldsby, alias Cherokee Bill, vs. The United States, No. 728, an indictment for the murder of Lawrence Keating. The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the lower court in the former case No. 620, for the murder of Ernest Melton. If the judgment in the case No. 620 has been carried out, and the plaintiff in error is now dead, the case No. 728 should be stricken from the docket of the Supreme Court. Please advise me of the fact as to whether Goldsby has been executed or not. Respectfully, Holwes Conrad, Solicitor General."

photographs.alt: The Hamilton Grange Dining Room. Featured in this room is a large table draped in a white tablecloth. On the table are plates, silver wear, glasses, and a silver mirrored island. Atop that are candle sticks, flowers, and a centerpiece adorned with grapes. On one side of the room are three triple hung floor-to-ceiling windows, draped with dainty white curtains. Across the room are three large doors. On one wall, there are two painted portraits: one of Elizabeth, and the other, of Alexander Hamilton. Below these portraits are two serving tables, holding porcelain pots, a silver wear case, glasses, tea ware, and a wine cooler. Across from this wall is a mantle atop which is a mirror.

photographs.alt: A group of early hadrosauroids, accompanied by a moderate-sized nodosaurid, walk through a coastal forest filled with ferns and early flowering plants (including relatives of modern sycamores and magnolias). A different, much larger nodosaurid (right) and a pair of dromaeosaurids (left) watch from the forest margins, while a goniopholidid ‘croc’ swims through the stream (bottom-left). An assortment of additional dinosaur footprints are recorded in the sediment, including those of other hadrosauroids and dromaeosaurids as well as a large predatory theropod (bottom-center). This scene takes place along the shoreline of the encroaching Western Interior Seaway that would soon cover much of North America, including western Colorado.
